paras: Today we look closely at the world around us, read a poem about the Sun, play word games and become young scientists to find out where the Sun goes at night.
Picture reading: Look at the picture carefully before you answer the questions.

sections.heading: A. Look at the picture and answer.
sections.note: Teacher note: Provide ample time to foster the skill of observation. Answers marked below follow the planned picture, so check them against the final picture you use.

items.q: 1. What can you see on both sides of the street?
items.a: Teacher note: Shops, a food stall, houses, dustbins and people walking. Accept any correct answer based on the picture.

items.q: 2. Why are there two dustbins? Do you know why one is blue and the other is green in colour?
items.a: Waste is kept separate. The green dustbin is for wet waste (vegetable peels, leftover food) and the blue dustbin is for dry waste (paper, plastic, tins). Teacher note: Colours can differ from place to place. Explain why we separate waste.

items.q: 3. Why is the man in dark glasses holding a white stick?
items.a: He cannot see well. The white stick helps him feel the way ahead, and it tells other people to help and give him space.

items.q: 4. Do you know which toy the boys are playing with?
items.a: They are playing with spinning tops. (Teacher note: Let children share the local name, for example, lattu or bambaram.)

items.q: 5. How many bullock-carts are there in the picture?
items.a: 2 bullock-carts in the planned picture. Teacher note: Ask children to count in the final picture.

items.q: 6. Name the different animals in the picture.
items.a: Bullocks, a dog, goats and a cat.

sections.heading: Science Corner: Everyday science on the street

items.q: Write wet waste or dry waste: banana peel, newspaper, plastic bottle, vegetable peels, leftover rice.
items.a: Banana peel - wet; newspaper - dry; plastic bottle - dry; vegetable peels - wet; leftover rice - wet.

items.q: The boys spin their tops. Why does a spinning top stay up while it spins but fall down after some time?
items.a: Spinning helps it balance. It slows down because the ground and air rub against it (friction), and then it falls. Teacher note: Accept simple answers such as 'it slows down'.

items.q: When the boy rings the bicycle bell, we hear a sound. What does the bell do to make the sound?
items.a: It shakes very fast (vibrates). Teacher note: Let children press a ruler on a desk edge, pluck it and feel it shake, or touch a stretched rubber band.

sections.heading: Maths Corner: Count the street
sections.note: Teacher note: These answers follow the planned picture. Change them if your final picture is different.

items.q: There are 2 bullock-carts and 1 bicycle. How many vehicles are there in all?
items.a: 2 + 1 = 3 vehicles.

items.q: A bullock-cart has 2 wheels and a bicycle has 2 wheels. How many wheels are there in all?
items.a: (2 x 2) + 2 = 6 wheels.

items.q: There are 2 spinning tops and 2 dustbins. Are there more tops or more dustbins? How many more?
items.a: They are equal, so there is no difference.

paras:
The sun that shines all day so bright,
I wonder where it goes at night.
It sinks behind a distant hill
And all the world grows dark and still.

And then I go to bed and sleep
Until the day begins to peep.
And when my eyes open,
I see the Sun is shining down on me.
Look at the picture. The Sun gives us light and heat. Plants, animals and people all need the Sun.

items.q: 1. Where does the Sun go after the end of the day?
items.a: In the poem, the Sun sinks behind a distant hill. Teacher note: The Sun does not really go anywhere. We will find out why in the Science Corner at the end of this lesson.

items.q: 2. Which among the following needs the Sun? Why? a) sunflower b) toys c) plants d) table e) children
items.a: Sunflower, plants and children need the Sun. Plants need sunlight to make food and grow. Children need sunlight to stay healthy and active. Toys and tables do not need the Sun.

items.q: 3. The poem talks about the Sun in the sky. What else do you see when you look up at the sky?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, clouds, birds, the Moon, stars, kites, aeroplanes, a rainbow).

items.q: 1. What different colours do we get to see during sunrise and sunset?
items.a: Teacher note: Red, orange, yellow, pink and purple. Let children say what they have seen.

items.q: 2. What do you see when you look at the sky at night?
items.a: Teacher note: The Moon, stars, and sometimes clouds. Accept other correct answers.

items.q: 3. How do you feel when you open your eyes in the morning?
items.a: Teacher note: Open-ended. Accept any honest answer with a reason.

items.q: 4. Imagine a day when the Sun doesn’t come out. Talk about how the day would be.
items.a: Teacher note: Sample: It would be dark and cold. Plants would not grow well, and wet clothes would not dry. Accept other sensible answers.

paras: Let’s play a fun game called “I Spy”! We are going to take turns to be Spies. The Spy secretly chooses something in the room and gives everyone a clue. The Spy starts by saying, ‘I spy with my little eye something that is ...’ and gives a clue. For example, ‘I spy something that is blue!’ Then, everyone looks around and tries to find something that is blue. Maybe it’s a pen, a chair, or even someone’s shirt!

If it’s tricky to guess the object right, the Spy can give more clues. The child who guesses right becomes the new Spy! Keep playing, taking turns being Spies and guessing until everyone gets a chance to be the Spy.
Let us speak. Read the following sentence: I spy a few stars in the sky.

The word spy begins with sp.
The word stars begins with st.
The word sky begins with sk.

sections.heading: D. Let us play “I Spy”.
sections.note: Teacher note: Model the game first. Give a clue and let children guess. Ask each child to give at least two clues, for example, colour first and then shape or size.

items.q: I spy something that is blue. Name three things in your classroom that are blue.
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, a pen, a bag, a shirt, a chair).

items.q: Now give a clue about something round or something that begins with ‘s’.
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, a clock, a ball, a slate, a shoe).

sections.heading: E. Now say these words aloud.
sections.note: Teacher note: Emphasise the pronunciation of the blends ‘sp’, ‘st’ and ‘sk’. Allow time for students to familiarise themselves with the sounds. Words from the book: Star, Storm, Store, Stain, Stick, Stair, Spoon, Splash, Spin, Skin, Skate, Sky.

items.q: Read these ‘sp’ words aloud: spot, spider, spell, speak, spend.
items.a: Teacher note: Say each word slowly, then fast. Let children clap once for each word.

items.q: Read these ‘st’ words aloud: stop, stamp, stone, step, stove.
items.a: Teacher note: Say each word slowly, then fast.

items.q: Read these ‘sk’ words aloud: skip, skirt, sketch, skunk, ski.
items.a: Teacher note: Say each word slowly, then fast.

sections.heading: F. Fill in the blanks with ‘sp’, ‘st’ or ‘sk’.

items.q: 1. ____ider
items.a: sp (spider)
st (stamp)
sk (skirt)
sp (spot)
sk (skip)
st (stone)

items.q: 7. ____etch
items.a: sk (sketch)
sp (spell)

sections.heading: G. Write a sentence of your own using one ‘sp’, one ‘st’ and one ‘sk’ word.

items.q: Use one word from each group in a sentence about the sky or the Sun.
items.a: Teacher note: Accept any correct sentence. Sample: I spot a star in the sky. The skater stops under the sun.

paras: Let us learn. Words can be joined together to make new words. Sun + light makes Sunlight. The Sun also gives its name to many other words. Let us find the words that belong to the sky and make new words with ‘Sun’.

sections.heading: H. Read the following words and circle the words that are found in the sky.
sections.note: Teacher note: Write the words on the board and let children circle them.

items.q: Stars   Storm   Store   Stain
items.a: Stars, Storm

items.q: Sun   Bicycle   Moon   Rain
items.a: Sun, Moon, Rain

items.q: Clouds   Flowers   Rainbow   Monkeys
items.a: Clouds, Rainbow

items.q: Computer   Shoes
items.a: None of these is found in the sky.

sections.heading: I. Add ‘Sun’ to the following words to make new words. Write them in the space given. One has been done for you.
sections.note: Words: light, flower, rays, set, rise, glasses, day. Example: Sunlight.

items.q: Sun + light
items.a: Sunlight (done for you)

items.q: Sun + flower
items.a: Sunflower

items.q: Sun + rays
items.a: Sunrays

items.q: Sun + set
items.a: Sunset

items.q: Sun + rise
items.a: Sunrise

items.q: Sun + glasses
items.a: Sunglasses

items.q: Sun + day
items.a: Sunday

items.q: Add ‘moon’ to light and beam to make two new words.
items.a: Moonlight, moonbeam.

items.q: Add ‘rain’ to bow and drop to make two new words. Which one is a sky word?
items.a: Rainbow, raindrop. Rainbow is found in the sky.

items.q: Add ‘star’ to fish and light to make two new words.
items.a: Starfish, starlight.

paras: The poem asked, “I wonder where it goes at night.” Let us become young scientists and find out. For these activities you will need a torch, a ball, a small sticker, a stick, a few clear cups, black and white paper, and two small plants or seedlings. Never look directly at the Sun, because it can hurt your eyes. Your teacher will guide you.

sections.heading: Physics Corner: Day and night
sections.note: Teacher note: Darken the room. Let the torch be the Sun and the ball be the Earth. Stick a small sticker on the ball to show where we live. Shine the torch on the ball from one side. Slowly turn the ball so the sticker moves from the lit side to the dark side and back again.

items.q: What does the torch stand for? What does the ball stand for?
items.a: The torch stands for the Sun and the ball stands for the Earth.

items.q: When the sticker is in the light, is it day or night at that place? And when it moves into the dark?
items.a: In the light it is day, and in the dark it is night.

items.q: Does the Sun really go down behind the hill at night? What really happens?
items.a: No. The Sun stays where it is. The Earth turns round like a top, and our place turns away from the Sun, so it becomes night.

items.q: The Earth takes one day, that is 24 hours, to turn around once. In the morning we see the Sun rise in the east. In which direction does the Sun set?
items.a: In the west. (Teacher note: The Sun only looks like it moves because the Earth is turning.)

items.q: Is the Sun a planet, a star or a moon?
items.a: A star. It looks big and bright because it is much closer to us than other stars.

sections.heading: Physics Corner: Shadows
sections.note: Teacher note: In the school ground, fix a stick upright in the ground or hold it in a pot of sand. Mark the end of its shadow with chalk in the morning, at noon and in the evening. If the Sun is not shining, shine a torch on the stick instead. Never look directly at the Sun.

items.q: What makes a shadow? Why does a shadow form behind a stick?
items.a: A shadow forms when an object blocks light. The light cannot go through the stick, so a dark shape forms behind it.

items.q: At which time of the day is the shadow the longest, and when is it the shortest?
items.a: The shadow is longest in the morning and in the evening, and shortest at noon when the Sun is high up in the sky. Children should record what they actually measure.

items.q: Name three things that make a shadow.
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary (for example, a tree, a person, a book, a building). Clear glass makes a very faint shadow.

sections.heading: Heat Corner: Light colours and dark colours
sections.note: Teacher note: Wrap one cup of water in black paper and another cup of water in white paper. Keep both in sunlight for about an hour. Then feel the water or use a thermometer. The black cup usually feels warmer.

items.q: Which cup of water became warmer, the one in black paper or the one in white paper?
items.a: Usually the cup in black paper. Children should record what they actually observe.

items.q: Why do we prefer light-coloured cotton clothes in summer?
items.a: Light colours reflect more sunlight, so we feel cooler. Dark colours take in more heat.

items.q: Wet clothes dry faster in the Sun. Why?
items.a: The heat of the Sun turns the water in the clothes into vapour, which goes into the air.

sections.heading: Biology Corner: Plants need sunlight
sections.note: Teacher note: Put one small plant in a sunny place and another in a dark cupboard. Give both the same amount of water. Look at them after a week. The plant in the dark usually turns pale and weak.

items.q: After a week, which plant is healthier, the one in the Sun or the one in the dark?
items.a: The plant in the Sun. The plant in the dark is usually pale and weak. Children should record what they actually observe.

items.q: Plants use sunlight, water and air to make their own food. Name something else in the poem or the picture that needs the Sun.
items.a: Teacher note: Sunflowers, children, animals, crops. Accept other sensible answers.

sections.heading: Sky Corner: Sun, Moon and stars

items.q: Which of these gives its own light: the Sun, the Moon or a star?
items.a: The Sun and a star. The Moon does not make its own light. It shines because sunlight falls on it.

items.q: How many colours are there in a rainbow? When can we see a rainbow?
items.a: 7 colours. We can see a rainbow when sunlight shines through raindrops, usually after rain with the Sun behind us.

items.q: Why can we not see the stars in the daytime?
items.a: The Sun is so bright that its light hides the faint light of the stars. The stars are still there.

sections.heading: Maths Corner: Hours, clocks and counting

items.q: On a day in the school year, the Sun rises at 6 a.m. and sets at 6 p.m. How many hours of daylight are there?
items.a: 6 a.m. to 12 noon is 6 hours, and 12 noon to 6 p.m. is 6 hours. 6 + 6 = 12 hours.

items.q: A day and a night together make 24 hours. If daylight is 12 hours, how many hours of night are there?
Meera goes to bed at 9 p.m. and wakes up at 6 a.m. How many hours does she sleep?
items.a: From 9 p.m. to 12 midnight is 3 hours, and from 12 midnight to 6 a.m. is 6 hours. 3 + 6 = 9 hours.

items.q: Draw a Sun with 8 rays. If you draw a line through the middle, how many rays are on each half?
items.a: 4 rays on each half (8 divided by 2 = 4).

items.q: Weather chart: For one week, tick sunny, cloudy or rainy each day. Make tally marks. Which kind of day was the most?
items.a: Teacher note: Answers will vary. Help children count the tally marks and, if time permits, draw a simple bar chart.
